source.title: Designing Role Vectors to Improve LLM Inference Behaviour
source.authors: Daniele Potertì; Andrea Seveso; Fabio Mercorio

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies role-specific activation directions and their effects on benchmark performance, but does not test overlapping sparse features, capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE feature recovery or completeness, or the dimensionality of features in superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports role-vector steering, ablation, and role-interpretation results. These bear on internal directions in LLMs but do not measure the representation properties named by any claim version. Cited results from other work were not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study builds difference-in-means role directions in instruction-tuned LLMs and measures MMLU changes under steering and ablation, plus judge-rated interpretability. It never measures sparse-feature overlap, capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE recovery or completeness, or feature dimensionality. It cites Toy Models and links scale-dependent interpretability to Templeton et al.'s monosemanticity only as interpretation.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that role-vector activation addition improves target-domain performance while largely preserving general capability. The effect depends on model scale and intervention depth. Only a subset (16% overall) of improving directions are judged to reflect the intended role.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses difference-in-means role directions from LLM activations, then activation addition and directional ablation on instruction-tuned LLMs; it does not use the original toy-model superposition setup or measure sparse-feature geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to model scale and intervention depth; it evaluates α=1 and α=3 and describes differing outcomes across roles and domains.

fits_no_version.finding: Judge-rated share of performance-improving role directions that match the intended role rises with size within families (e.g., Gemma-2 17%→30%, Qwen 6%→15%). The authors read this as more monosemantic representations at scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger LLMs yield steering directions more interpretable as specific concepts than smaller models in the same family.

fits_no_version.finding: Role directions added via activation addition change domain MMLU accuracy in Qwen-7B-Chat, and ablating them often cuts performance broadly, by up to about 70% in some roles.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Difference-in-means role directions causally affect LLM benchmark performance in a role- and domain-dependent way.

record.problems: The paper states that exact semantic interpretation of the directions remains uncertain and that results may differ in untested, especially larger, models. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated outcomes. Full experimental results are said to be in supplementary materials available to reviewers, not in the provided text.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; 13 rows record the explicit related direction-steering and interpretation findings. Detailed Table 3 and Table 5 results for individual role-by-domain combinations were not extracted because they do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: All: toy networks, sparsity, near-orthogonal overlap, phase transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition as the cause of polysemantic neurons.
All: no measure of features distributed across neurons, and no SAE recovery.
All: dimensionality of superposed features is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: No bearing on any superposition version. The reference to Toy Models is citation-only. The monosemanticity-with-scale remark is the authors' interpretation of patch-scoping rates, not a superposition measurement.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity, overlap, near-orthogonality, and sparsity-dependent geometric transitions.
Whether feature competition for limited capacity causes polysemantic neurons or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Whether features are distributed across neurons or sparse features are recoverable with a dictionary such as an SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of model representations.
Whether the features represented in superposition are one-dimensional rather than multi-dimensional.
